cleaned_entries.title: Production 3-tier web architecture on AWS
cleaned_entries.content:
Production 3-tier web architecture on AWS

The baseline reference: ALB in public subnets across 3 AZs → ECS/EKS application tier in private subnets across 3 AZs → RDS Multi-AZ in isolated data subnets. WAF in front of the ALB, CloudFront for static assets and edge caching, S3 for object storage, ElastiCache for session/cache. Every tier has its own Security Group, referencing the SG of the tier above it (web-sg → app-sg → db-sg). This is the safe default for any web-style workload — if you do not have a strong reason to deviate, ship this.

Decision rules:
- DEPLOY across 3 AZs minimum for production (2 AZs is staging)
- USE ALB for HTTP(S), NLB for TCP/UDP or extreme throughput, API Gateway for serverless / fine-grained throttling
- ENABLE WAF managed rule sets (AWS Managed Rules Common, Known Bad Inputs, SQLi)
- PUT CloudFront in front of any externally-facing endpoint — DDoS protection (Shield Standard) + edge cache + lower data-transfer cost
- RDS Multi-AZ for production; consider Aurora over RDS for >100GB databases or read-replica-heavy workloads

Trade-offs:
- 3 AZs: max availability vs higher NAT gateway and data-transfer cost
- Aurora vs RDS: better performance and HA vs higher cost and AWS-only
- ALB vs API Gateway: ALB cheaper and lower-latency vs API Gateway has built-in throttling, auth, mappings

Anti-patterns:
- Single-AZ deployment for production — one AZ event takes the service down
- Public IPs on application instances 'for SSH' — use Session Manager
- RDS in a public subnet 'so the BI team can connect' — use a bastion or AWS Client VPN

cleaned_entries.title: Production EKS topology for microservice workloads
cleaned_entries.content:
Production EKS topology for microservice workloads

EKS managed control plane in 3 AZs; managed node groups (mix of On-Demand and Spot) provisioned by Karpenter; AWS VPC CNI for pod networking; AWS Load Balancer Controller for ALB/NLB ingress; ExternalDNS for Route 53; cert-manager for TLS; Argo CD for GitOps; OpenTelemetry Collector as DaemonSet; Falco for runtime detection; OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for policy. IRSA for workload IAM. NetworkPolicy default-deny per namespace. Secrets via External Secrets Operator from AWS Secrets Manager.

Decision rules:
- ONE production cluster per region per environment — multi-tenancy via namespaces, not multi-cluster, until ~500 services
- USE Karpenter for node provisioning, not Cluster Autoscaler — better Spot diversification and bin-packing
- GITOPS (Argo CD or Flux) is the only path to apply manifests in prod — kubectl apply by humans is forbidden
- ENFORCE PodSecurityStandard `restricted` in every workload namespace; `baseline` only for kube-system
- RUN admission policy (Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper) blocking: privileged pods, hostPath, default ServiceAccount usage, missing resource requests

Trade-offs:
- Karpenter: faster, denser packing vs newer than Cluster Autoscaler
- Argo CD vs Flux: Argo has a UI and is the de facto standard; Flux is leaner and more modular
- AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB per Ingress) vs nginx ingress (one ALB, host-based routing): ALB-per-Ingress isolates blast radius; nginx is cheaper at scale

Anti-patterns:
- One giant cluster for prod and non-prod — blast radius is unacceptable
- Helm chart per-team without a central platform team — consistency and security policy drift
- Skipping admission policy — security guardrails as code review only is unreliable

cleaned_entries.title: AWS landing zone with Organizations, Control Tower, and SCPs
cleaned_entries.content:
AWS landing zone with Organizations, Control Tower, and SCPs

A multi-account strategy is the strongest blast-radius control AWS offers. Use AWS Organizations with Control Tower to bootstrap: a Management account (billing, Organizations only — never run workloads here), Log Archive (immutable CloudTrail/Config logs), Audit (read-only security tooling), and per-team / per-environment workload accounts (dev/staging/prod separated). Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce guardrails that even account admins cannot bypass.

Decision rules:
- ONE production account per business unit / per environment — not 'one prod account for everything'
- MANAGEMENT account runs no workloads — only billing, Organizations, and Identity Center (SSO)
- LOG ARCHIVE account is the centralized destination for CloudTrail (org trail), Config, and S3 access logs — immutable bucket policy with object lock
- SCPs at the OU level enforce guardrails: deny disabling CloudTrail/Config, deny region usage outside approved list, deny IAM user creation, deny S3 public-access toggle
- USE AWS Identity Center (SSO) with permission sets mapped to SAML/OIDC IdP groups — no IAM users in workload accounts

Trade-offs:
- More accounts: stronger isolation vs more accounts to manage — Control Tower and Account Factory automate the long tail
- Strict SCPs: tight guardrails vs frustration when a legit need is blocked — use OUs to scope SCPs
- Centralized logging: clean audit vs cross-account log shipping cost

Anti-patterns:
- Running workloads in the management account — privilege concentration disaster
- One IAM user per developer per account — Identity Center exists for a reason
- SCPs that allow * — provides no guardrail

cleaned_entries.title: RTO/RPO patterns: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Region Active-Active
cleaned_entries.content:
RTO/RPO patterns: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Region Active-Active

DR strategy is a function of acceptable downtime (RTO) and acceptable data loss (RPO). The four canonical AWS DR strategies trade cost for recovery speed: Backup & Restore (RTO hours, cheapest), Pilot Light (RTO ~1h, core infra running, app dormant), Warm Standby (RTO minutes, scaled-down replica running), Multi-Region Active-Active (RTO seconds, expensive). Most workloads do not need active-active; matching DR to actual business RTO/RPO saves significant cost.

Decision rules:
- DEFINE RTO/RPO from the business owner — not from the engineering wishlist
- BACKUP & RESTORE for non-critical workloads (RTO 4-24h, RPO hours): AWS Backup, cross-region copy
- PILOT LIGHT for critical-but-not-tier-0 (RTO 1-4h, RPO minutes): keep VPC, RDS read-replica, IAM in DR region; spin up app on failover
- WARM STANDBY for tier-1 (RTO 5-30m, RPO seconds): scaled-down full stack in DR region, scale up on failover
- ACTIVE-ACTIVE for tier-0 (RTO seconds, RPO sub-second): Aurora Global / DynamoDB Global Tables, Route 53 latency routing
- TEST DR quarterly with real failover — untested DR is not DR

Trade-offs:
- Active-active: lowest RTO vs highest cost (~2x) and data-consistency complexity (conflict resolution)
- Pilot Light: cheap insurance vs requires automation that has been rehearsed
- Cross-region backup: cheap vs RTO measured in hours — only acceptable for non-critical data

Anti-patterns:
- Single-region 'Multi-AZ is enough' for tier-0 — regional outages happen (us-east-1 has had several)
- DR plan that has never been tested — first failover during a real incident is the worst time to find bugs
- Active-active without conflict-resolution strategy — silent data corruption

cleaned_entries.title: Hybrid connectivity: Direct Connect, VPN, and Outposts
cleaned_entries.content:
Hybrid connectivity: Direct Connect, VPN, and Outposts

Hybrid is common for regulated industries, large existing on-prem footprints, or data-sovereignty constraints. AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the public internet is fast to set up but limited to ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel and depends on internet. Direct Connect provides dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps with predictable latency but takes weeks to provision and requires colo presence. Use Direct Connect + VPN as backup. AWS Outposts extends the AWS control plane into your data center for true hybrid workloads.

Decision rules:
- USE Site-to-Site VPN for ≤1 Gbps, dev/staging hybrid, or as Direct Connect backup
- USE Direct Connect for production hybrid: ≥1 Gbps sustained, latency-sensitive, or compliance prohibits internet path
- ALWAYS pair Direct Connect with VPN backup — DX outages do happen
- ATTACH DX/VPN to Transit Gateway, not directly to a VPN gateway — TGW scales to many VPCs
- USE Outposts when latency-critical workloads must be on-prem AND you want the AWS control plane (rare; expensive)

Trade-offs:
- Direct Connect: predictable performance vs weeks to provision, monthly port fee
- Multiple DX connections (different locations): true HA vs more cost
- Outposts: AWS-native hybrid vs expensive, capacity-locked

Anti-patterns:
- Single Direct Connect with no VPN backup — single fiber cut takes the link down
- Hybrid via internet VPN for production payment workloads — latency and reliability are not enough
- VPN to a single VPN Gateway when scaling beyond 2-3 VPCs — TGW is the right primitive
